title: Ray Summit 2026: Physical AI, RL, and the infrastructure that runs them all | Anyscale
gist: Ray Summit 2026 framed reinforcement learning as having graduated from a research topic into a production engineering problem, with speaker after speaker (NVIDIA, Torc Robotics, Lila Sciences, Periodic Labs, Bedrock Robotics, Microsoft AI, Spotify, Capital One, Recursion) showing 10-50x infrastructure efficiency gains from consolidating fragmented training/inference stacks onto Ray.

insights.claim: Reinforcement learning has moved from a research topic into a production engineering problem, where the infrastructure holding RL pipelines together is now as consequential as the models it trains.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Investors should track RL infrastructure vendors (Anyscale/Ray, inference stacks) as a distinct value pool from model providers, since compute orchestration is becoming a bottleneck and differentiator in its own right.
insights.quote: reinforcement learning has graduated from a research topic into a production engineering problem, and the infrastructure that holds RL pipelines together is now as consequential as the models it trains.

insights.claim: Frontier AI workloads today combine continuous RL training loops, agentic rollouts, and physical simulation at scale, all of which require compute environments spanning heterogeneous hardware and coordinating CPU workers with GPU pools while recovering from failures automatically.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous compute orchestration (not raw GPU count) is becoming a gating factor for frontier AI development, favoring platforms that abstract across CPU/GPU/accelerator fleets.

themes.theme: Verifier economics in scientific RL (Lila Sciences)

insights.claim: RLVR (RL with verifiable rewards) has succeeded in coding and math because those domains have cheap, automatic verifiers, but only about 5% of biology, chemistry, and materials science literature contains claims that can be fully settled in silico.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: The scarcity of in-silico-verifiable claims in physical science is the structural reason AI progress in biotech/materials lags coding/math, and explains why capital is now flowing into physical 'verifier' infrastructure (robotic labs) rather than just larger models.
insights.quote: only about 5% of bio, chem, and materials literature contains claims that can be settled fully in silico

insights.claim: Lila Sciences built a 15,000-square-foot 'AI Science Factory' in Cambridge that wraps every lab instrument behind a single API and runs robotics-driven experiments around the clock, turning the physical workcell itself into the reward signal for its IRIS model.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Physical automated labs-as-reward-signal is a capital-intensive but potentially defensible moat for AI-driven drug/materials discovery firms; watch for similar 'foundry' builds from competitors.

insights.claim: Lila's CAR-T program reached non-human primate efficacy data at roughly 30 times lower cost than conventional development timelines.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: A 30x cost reduction in preclinical biologics development, if replicated, would materially compress biotech R&D cost curves and timelines for cell-therapy pipelines.

insights.claim: Lila designed and tested more than one million mRNAs in vivo against leading clinical benchmarks, and screened 719 protective coating alloys in five weeks versus a conventional seven months.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Roughly 6x faster materials-screening cycles suggest AI-robotic labs could compress industrial R&D timelines beyond biotech into coatings/materials science broadly.

themes.theme: Physical AI and autonomy at scale (Torc Robotics, Bedrock Robotics)

insights.claim: Urban self-driving benchmarks are saturating, and the harder unsolved problems in autonomy have shifted to long-haul trucking, which requires ultra-long-range detection, high ego speeds, and trajectory lengths that existing public datasets were not built to cover.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Capital and competitive focus in autonomy is rotating from robotaxi/urban AV toward autonomous trucking, where Torc's proprietary TruckDrive dataset creates a data moat.
insights.locator: Felix Heide, Head of AI, Torc Robotics

insights.claim: Torc's Alpamayo planning model achieves a min-of-6 Average Displacement Error of 5.84 meters at a 6.4-second horizon zero-shot, which drops to 0.87 meters when a physical AI reasoning trace is added — roughly a 6.7x accuracy improvement.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Chain-of-thought-style reasoning traces materially improve trajectory prediction accuracy in autonomous trucking, suggesting reasoning-augmented planning models are becoming table stakes in AV.

insights.claim: By consolidating five separate training systems onto a single Ray cluster spanning CPU nodes, Kepler GPUs, and Blackwell GPUs on Anyscale, Torc achieved 20 times more data per training job, 3-3.4 times faster epochs on cheaper compute, GPU utilization rising from 30-40% to approximately 90%, and one billion simulation miles run per week.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: GPU utilization near 90% (vs. 30-40% baseline) implies large latent compute efficiency gains available industry-wide simply from orchestration consolidation, independent of new hardware spend.

insights.claim: Bedrock Robotics' core insight is that job-site construction data is fundamentally unlike task-defined robotics data: unlike pick-and-place systems where the task is defined before data collection, figuring out what happened on a job site is itself the output of a distributed compute graph run on Ray.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Construction/heavy-equipment autonomy requires fundamentally different data-labeling infrastructure than warehouse or urban-driving robotics, a distinct sub-market with its own compute requirements.

insights.claim: The inference problem has become combinatorial: the vLLM community now navigates more than 1,000 hardware configurations and more than 5,000 models, with workload patterns shifting from single-turn completions to multi-turn agentic interactions.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Fragmentation across hardware and models is a growing tax on inference providers, reinforcing the value of a common serving abstraction layer like vLLM as a chokepoint/platform play.

insights.claim: vLLM has grown to more than 3,000 contributors and is investing in day-zero hardware support for NVIDIA Blackwell and Vera Rubin, AMD MI355X and MI455X, and Google Ironwood and future TPU generations, positioning it as one of the central open inference substrates in the AI ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: vLLM's cross-vendor day-zero support strategy makes it a de facto neutral inference layer, reducing switching costs between GPU/TPU vendors and potentially compressing hardware vendors' margins on lock-in.

insights.claim: Agentic API, a new Rust-based serving layer built on vLLM, provides shared infrastructure for restoring conversation history, running multi-call tool loops, and persisting agent state — supporting both the OpenAI Responses API and Anthropic Messages API so that clients like Codex and Claude Code can use open models served by vLLM without building their own state layer.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: A shared agent-state serving layer compatible with both major agent API formats lowers switching costs between closed and open models for agentic products, accelerating open-model adoption in agent tooling.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra model has 550 billion total parameters with 55 billion active and was trained on over 20 trillion pretraining tokens, requiring RL coordination of rollout engines, environment workers, and policy training across more than 3,000 GPUs simultaneously on Ray Core.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: A 550B-parameter open-weight model with a 10:1 sparsity ratio (55B active) trained at 3,000+ GPU scale on Ray signals NVIDIA is directly competing with closed frontier labs while also validating Ray as a frontier-scale RL substrate.

insights.claim: A topology-aware placement change on GB300 hardware — keeping communicating RL actors within the same NVLink domain — improved RL iteration throughput by 13% with no changes to hardware or model.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Double-digit throughput gains from pure scheduling/placement optimization show meaningful 'free' efficiency still exists in large-scale RL training even on cutting-edge hardware.

insights.claim: NVIDIA reported that customers using Nemotron-derived models saw concrete downstream gains: CrowdStrike completed security investigations up to five times faster, Synopsys reached validated RTL up to 50 times faster, and CodeRabbit improved routing accuracy while cutting estimated serving costs in half.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: These vendor-reported multiples are the kind of ROI data points enterprise buyers use to justify open-model adoption over proprietary APIs; if verified independently they strengthen the case for NVIDIA's open-model strategy.

insights.claim: NVIDIA frames Nemotron as a full open suite — model checkpoints, a 9-trillion-token dataset published on Hugging Face, and open libraries for RL alignment (NeMo-RL), compression (Minitron), and architecture search — explicitly designed so any organization can build AI specialized on its own data.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is commoditizing the model layer to protect and grow its compute/infrastructure layer — a strategic pattern investors should recognize when evaluating NVIDIA's competitive moat versus pure model vendors.

themes.theme: Physical-world RL is structurally harder (Periodic Labs)

insights.claim: Running RL in the physical world is harder than in digital domains because rollouts take days rather than minutes, fewer agents can run in parallel, and reward signals are noisier.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Physical-science RL companies face structurally slower iteration cycles than software RL, implying longer paths to ROI and a premium on infrastructure that compresses each cycle.

insights.claim: Periodic Labs draws a distinction between AI that 'knows science' and AI that 'knows how to do science,' and trains its model on the scientific process itself — hypotheses, experimental plans, tool invocations, measurements, and the updates those measurements produce — rather than on the finished record of published results.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Training on process rather than published output is a distinct data strategy that could differentiate 'AI scientist' companies from those simply fine-tuning on scientific literature.

insights.claim: Periodic Labs' custom stack (Ray for orchestration, Megatron for training, SGLang for inference, plus proprietary RL, GPU-colocated sandboxes, and serving layers) benchmarks at 3x inference throughput, 10x faster weight sync, 30x faster weight conversion, 4.5x faster overall training, and a job-local P2P data plane 50 times faster than comparable SOTA providers versus open-source baselines.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: These are vendor-claimed multiples versus open-source baselines rather than independently verified benchmarks, but if accurate they represent a meaningful infrastructure moat for AI-scientist startups over off-the-shelf stacks.

insights.claim: Microsoft AI's legacy Ray Client proxy degraded severely at scale: actor creation time rose from 42.6 seconds at 8,000 workers to 89.4 seconds at 32,000 workers, and steady-state P99 RPC latency grew from 18.3 to 55.3 seconds over the same range.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: This quantifies a real scaling ceiling in Ray's default GCS proxy architecture at tens-of-thousands-of-worker scale, which matters for any organization planning frontier-scale RL clusters.
insights.locator: Cheng Liu, Paweł Bęza, Shaowei Su, Microsoft AI

insights.claim: Microsoft AI's RELAY batch proxy fixed this bottleneck, holding actor creation time between 32.7 and 34.5 seconds across the full range (2.85x faster at 32,000 workers) and steady-state RPC at approximately 3.6 seconds (16.4x faster at 32,000 workers), using a hierarchical relay tree that reduces driver-side cost from O(K×S) to O(S).
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: A 16x latency improvement at 32k-worker scale is a substantial open-source-adjacent contribution that likely raises the practical ceiling for Ray-based RL clusters industry-wide.

insights.claim: Spotify's Hendrix ML platform grew 2.5 times in supported teams and 30 times in GPU compute over the past year, now running more than one million GPU hours per month and roughly 21,000 batch LLM jobs monthly.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: A 30x compute growth rate in one year at a non-AI-native company like Spotify illustrates how quickly ML/AI compute demand is scaling even outside dedicated AI labs.

insights.claim: Capital One's transformer model for tabular financial event sequences (500M+ records, 3.5 terabytes across 512 timesteps) initially took 32 hours per training epoch due to data-loading bottlenecks; a unified KubeRay stack cut hyperparameter-optimization wall time from 3-5 days to approximately four hours, a 16x acceleration, running 200 concurrent experiments.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Data loading rather than compute being the bottleneck at a large financial institution highlights that orchestration/data-pipeline engineering, not GPU count, is often the binding constraint on enterprise AI velocity.

insights.claim: Recursion's key architectural principle for its drug-discovery platform is treating workloads rather than clusters as the unit of work, with routing decisions made on cost, availability, and data locality.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: Workload-centric (vs. cluster-centric) scheduling is emerging as a best-practice architecture pattern for multi-cloud AI infrastructure, relevant to any capital-intensive AI compute buyer optimizing cost.

insights.claim: Ray added two new APIs, SlicePlacementGroup and SubslicePlacementGroup, for managing TPU topology on Google Kubernetes Engine, enabling dynamic subdivision of large TPU slices without physical cluster reconfiguration, alongside elastic recovery and preemption handling for both JAX and PyTorch.
insights.speaker: Philip Wang
insights.so_what: First-class TPU support in Ray reduces switching costs between NVIDIA GPUs and Google TPUs for large training/inference workloads, a competitive pressure point on GPU vendor pricing power.
insights.locator: Ryan O'Leary, Lehui Liu, TPU on Ray session
